items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. The PRUDENT investor kept a third of her money in cash, refused to borrow for shares, and sold half her holding when the market doubled in a year.
items.explanation: Keeping cash in reserve, refusing to borrow and selling after a doubling are careful risk avoidance, not recklessness, generosity or indecision.

items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. An ARDENT supporter of the new library, she attended every council meeting, wrote to the local paper twice a week, and raised half the funds herself.
items.explanation: Attending every meeting, writing twice a week and raising half the funds is passion, not mild interest, opposition or indifference.

items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. The VIGILANT guard checked every vehicle twice, noted the number plates, and refused entry to anyone without a pass, even regular visitors.
items.explanation: Checking every vehicle twice and refusing entry without a pass is watchfulness, not carelessness, friendliness or tiredness.

items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. The FERVENT crowd cheered every goal, sang through the rain, and stayed until the last player left the field.
items.explanation: Cheering every goal, singing through rain and staying until the end is passionate intensity, not restraint, boredom or hostility.

items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. The DILIGENT clerk verified every entry twice, traced each discrepancy to its source, and finished the audit a day early.
items.explanation: Verifying every entry twice and tracing each discrepancy is hard, careful work, not laziness, sloppiness or dishonesty.

items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. The RESOLUTE captain refused to abandon the ship, ordered the crew to the lifeboats first, and stayed on the bridge until the last boat was away.
items.explanation: Refusing to abandon ship and staying until the last boat was away is determination, not panic, confusion or cruelty.

items.question: Read the sentence and choose the meaning of the word in capitals as it is used here. The AMIABLE shopkeeper greeted every customer by name, remembered their usual orders, and never once raised his voice in twenty years.
items.explanation: Greeting customers by name, remembering orders and never raising his voice is friendliness, not rudeness, shyness or strictness.

items.question: Read the four sentences and choose the one that is grammatically correct.
options: The data shows that the new drug works, and each trial have been independently reviewed.
The data show that the new drug works, and each trial has been independently reviewed.
The data show that the new drug works, and each trial have been independently reviewed.
The data shows that the new drug works, and each trial has been independently reviewed.
items.explanation: 'Data' is plural, so it takes 'show', and 'each' is singular, so it takes 'has been'. Only the second sentence gets both right.

items.question: Read the four sentences and choose the one that is grammatically correct.
options: Neither the manager nor the workers was informed, and the union has asked for a meeting.
Neither the manager nor the workers was informed, and the union have asked for a meeting.
Neither the manager nor the workers were informed, and the union has asked for a meeting.
Neither the manager nor the workers were informed, and the union have asked for a meeting.
items.explanation: The verb after 'neither... nor' agrees with the nearer subject, so 'workers' takes 'were', and 'the union' as one body takes 'has'. Only the second sentence gets both right.

items.question: Read the four sentences and choose the one that is grammatically correct.
options: The number of errors has fallen, and the committee are satisfied with the progress.
The number of errors have fallen, and the committee is satisfied with the progress.
The number of errors have fallen, and the committee are satisfied with the progress.
The number of errors has fallen, and the committee is satisfied with the progress.
items.explanation: 'The number' is singular, so it takes 'has', and the committee acts as one body, so it takes 'is'. Only the second sentence gets both right.

items.question: Read the four sentences and choose the one that is grammatically correct.
options: Each of the students has submitted the assignment, and neither the teacher nor the parents has seen the results yet.
Each of the students has submitted the assignment, and neither the teacher nor the parents have seen the results yet.
Each of the students have submitted the assignment, and neither the teacher nor the parents has seen the results yet.
Each of the students have submitted the assignment, and neither the teacher nor the parents have seen the results yet.
items.explanation: 'Each' is singular, so it takes 'has', and the verb after 'neither... nor' agrees with the nearer subject, so 'parents' takes 'have'. Only the third sentence gets both right.

items.passage:
Every time a person opens a free app, a bargain is struck, though neither side states its terms plainly. The user gets a service that would cost money to build and run, and the company gets data: location, contacts, browsing history, and the pattern of taps and pauses that reveals what holds attention. The user is told that consent has been given, because a box was ticked on a screen that appeared before the service could be used. Both sides then proceed as if a genuine agreement had been reached, when what actually happened was closer to a toll: pay with your data, or do not pass. The question is whether a tick given under those conditions can count as consent at all.
The defenders of the current system argue that users do understand the bargain and accept it. People know, they say, that free services are paid for with advertising, and advertising needs data. If users truly objected, they would stop using the services, and they do not. The fact that billions of people continue to use these apps is, on this view, evidence that the bargain is acceptable.  But knowing in general terms is not the same as knowing what is collected, who it is sold to, and what inferences are drawn from it. 
The law has tried to close this gap by requiring consent to be specific, informed and freely given. In practice, the requirement has produced consent screens of remarkable length and obscurity, written in legal language that few readers finish and fewer understand. Companies comply with the letter of the law by disclosing everything, and defeat its purpose by disclosing it in a form nobody can use. The result is consent fatigue: users click accept on everything, not because they agree, but because refusing means losing the service and reading the policy means losing the afternoon. 
There are better designs, and some are already in use. One is to make the default the most private setting, so that sharing requires an active choice rather than a failure to opt out. Another is to require consent separately for each purpose, so that agreeing to location for navigation does not also agree to location for advertising. A third is to limit how long data may be kept and to require its deletion on request, with the deletion verified rather than merely promised. Each of these shifts the burden from the user, who must currently defend her privacy against a system designed to erode it, to the company, which must justify each collection. None of them destroys the business model: advertising can work with less data, as the history of advertising before the internet shows, though it works less profitably.
The deeper issue is that data is not like money. Money spent is gone, but data given can be copied endlessly, combined with other data, and used years later for purposes nobody imagined when it was collected. Consent given today cannot sensibly cover uses invented tomorrow. That is why the strongest protection is not a better consent form but a limit on collection itself: collect only what the service needs, keep it only as long as it is needed, and do not sell it at all. Until the law draws that line, the tick box will remain what it is now: a ritual that protects the company far more than the user.
items.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the better consent designs proposed in the passage?
options: Make the most private setting the default, so sharing requires an active choice
Require consent separately for each purpose
Limit how long data may be kept and require its deletion on request, verified rather than merely promised
Make consent forms longer and more detailed
items.explanation: The passage proposes private-by-default settings, separate consent per purpose and limited retention with verified deletion. Longer and more detailed forms are the problem the passage describes, not a proposed design.

items.question: Which of the following statements are true according to the passage? (A) The passage implies that knowing free services are paid for by advertising does not mean users know what is collected or sold. (B) Consent screens defeat the law's purpose by disclosing everything in a form nobody can use. (C) The author believes a better consent form is the strongest protection available.
items.explanation: A is true: knowing in general terms is not the same as knowing what is collected, who it is sold to and what inferences are drawn. B is true: companies comply with the letter of the law by disclosing everything and defeat its purpose by disclosing it in a form nobody can use. C is false: the strongest protection is a limit on collection itself, not a better consent form.

items.question: In the passage, the phrase 'consent fatigue' means that
options: users click accept because they trust companies to collect only what is needed
users click accept because refusing would be illegal
users click accept on everything because refusing costs the service and reading costs too much time
users click accept because the screens are short and easy to understand
items.explanation: The passage defines the result: users click accept not because they agree, but because refusing means losing the service and reading the policy means losing the afternoon. The screens are long and obscure, not short, and trust and legality are not the reasons given.

items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the passage's claim that better consent designs will not destroy the advertising business model?
options: Many users value free services more than they fear data collection.
Some apps already use private-by-default settings.
Advertisers in a large trial paid almost nothing for ads targeted with limited data, because the ads reached almost no interested buyers.
Data brokers buy location records from apps.
items.explanation: The claim is that advertising can work with less data, though less profitably. If limited-data ads reach almost no interested buyers and advertisers pay almost nothing, the model does not merely earn less, it collapses, which attacks the claim's mechanism. The other options are facts the passage already accepts.

items.question: The author's main conclusion about data consent is that
options: consent forms should be made longer and more detailed.
free apps should be banned until users read their policies.
real protection requires limiting collection itself, since consent given today cannot cover uses invented tomorrow and data can be copied and reused endlessly.
users should stop using all free apps immediately.
items.explanation: The author concludes that the strongest protection is not a better consent form but a limit on collection: collect only what is needed, keep it briefly, and do not sell it. The other options state measures the author criticises or never proposes.

items.passage:
The shift from petrol cars to electric vehicles is usually described as a technology story: batteries got cheaper, ranges got longer, and charging got faster. The technology story is true, but it is not the whole story, and in India it may not even be the main story. The main story is infrastructure, and infrastructure is a coordination problem. A buyer will not buy an electric car without chargers nearby, and nobody will build chargers without electric cars nearby to use them. Each side waits for the other, and the market stays small. Governments break this circle by subsidising one side or the other, but subsidies are expensive, and they create their own problems: chargers built where they are not needed, and cars bought by people who would have bought them anyway.
The second part of the story is the grid. An electric car is, in effect, a large battery on wheels, and a city full of them is a large new demand on the electricity system. If most owners charge in the evening, when they return home, the evening peak grows sharply, and the grid must be strengthened at great cost. If owners can be persuaded to charge at night, when demand is low, the same cars become an asset, soaking up surplus power and even, in principle, feeding it back. The difference between these two futures is not technology but pricing and habit: charge more in the evening and less at night, and behaviour follows. Few Indian cities have yet put such pricing in place, and fewer still have explained it to consumers in a way that changes when they plug in.
The third part is the supply chain. A petrol car has an engine with hundreds of moving parts, made by a network of suppliers built over decades. An electric car has a battery, a motor and electronics, and the battery is the expensive part, dominated by a small number of countries that control the minerals and the processing. For India, which imports almost all of its oil, swapping dependence on oil exporters for dependence on battery exporters is an improvement but not an escape. The government's answer has been to subsidise battery manufacturing at home, but building that capacity takes years, and the technology changes while it is being built. A factory designed for one battery chemistry can be outdated before it opens.
None of this means the transition will fail. Electric two-wheelers, which need smaller batteries and shorter ranges, are already selling in large numbers, and they suit Indian cities, where most trips are short. Buses and three-wheelers, which run fixed routes and return to a depot every night, are even easier to electrify, and several cities have already begun. The passenger car, the vehicle the debate focuses on, is the hardest case, because it needs long range, fast charging and a large battery. The sensible sequence is therefore to electrify first where it is easiest, learn from those fleets, and let the car follow. A transition that starts with buses and scooters and ends with cars is less dramatic than one that starts with cars, but it is far more likely to arrive.
items.question: Which of the following is NOT given in the passage as a reason the passenger car is the hardest vehicle to electrify?
options: It needs a smaller battery than a two-wheeler
items.explanation: The passage says the passenger car needs long range, fast charging and a large battery. Two-wheelers need smaller batteries, so needing a smaller battery than a two-wheeler is the opposite of what the passage says.

items.question: Which of the following statements are true according to the passage? (A) The passage implies that the difference between a harmful evening peak and a useful night-time asset is pricing and habit, not battery technology. (B) Buses and three-wheelers are easier to electrify than cars because they run fixed routes and return to a depot nightly. (C) The author believes the transition will fail because battery manufacturing takes years to build.
items.explanation: A is true: the difference between the two futures is not technology but pricing and habit. B is true: buses and three-wheelers run fixed routes and return to a depot every night. C is false: the passage says none of this means the transition will fail.

items.question: In the passage, the word 'circle' in 'governments break this circle' refers to
options: the cycle in which subsidies create chargers that create buyers that justify more subsidies
the round trip a car makes between home and a charging station
the group of countries that control battery minerals
the waiting game in which buyers and charger builders each wait for the other
items.explanation: The passage describes the coordination problem as a circle in which each side waits for the other, and says governments break it by subsidising one side. Subsidies are the tool that breaks the circle, not a cycle that forms it, and the other options are not the sense used.

items.question: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the passage's claim that pricing can shift charging to the night?
options: Several cities have begun electrifying their buses.
Most owners currently charge in the evening.
In a city that introduced much cheaper night charging, the share of charging done at night rose from a fifth to two-thirds within a year.
Batteries have become cheaper over the last decade.
items.explanation: The claim is that pricing changes when people plug in. Evidence that cheaper night charging moved the night share from a fifth to two-thirds directly supports that mechanism. The other options are background facts that do not test pricing.

items.question: The author's main recommendation for electrifying transport is that
options: India should electrify first where it is easiest, buses, three-wheelers and two-wheelers, and let passenger cars follow.
passenger cars should be electrified before all other vehicles.
the transition should be abandoned because the grid cannot cope.
subsidies should be given only to car buyers.
items.explanation: The passage concludes that the sensible sequence is to electrify first where it is easiest, learn from those fleets, and let the car follow. The other options state the opposite sequence or outcomes the author rejects.

items.question: Choose the idiom that fits both sentences. (1) The startup had to ___ when funding dried up, cutting costs to the bone. (2) The family had to ___ after the harvest failed, selling the second tractor.
items.explanation: Both sentences describe cutting spending to survive a loss of income. 'Bite the dust' means failing outright, which neither did; the other two do not fit either sentence.

items.question: Choose the idiom that fits both sentences. (1) The two neighbours decided to ___ their dispute and share the cost of the fence. (2) The rival firms decided to ___ their patent fight and cross-license the technology.
items.explanation: Both sentences describe ending a dispute and cooperating afterwards. The other idioms describe enduring something unpleasant, avoiding a decision or evading a question, none of which fits.

items.question: Choose the idiom that fits both sentences. (1) The scandal dealt a ___ to the minister's reputation, which had taken twenty years to build. (2) The defeat dealt a ___ to the team's confidence before the final.
items.explanation: Both sentences describe damage to something valuable: a reputation and confidence. A helping hand is the opposite, and the other two phrases do not fit the sentence pattern.

items.question: A person who both studies birds in the wild and records their songs is called?
items.explanation: An ornithologist both studies birds in the wild and records their behaviour and songs. A zoologist studies all animals, a vet treats them, and a falconer trains falcons.

items.question: A large tank where fish are kept and displayed for the public is called?
items.explanation: An aquarium is a large tank where fish are kept and displayed for the public. A pond is natural and not for display, a net catches fish, and a hatchery breeds them.

items.question: A person who both donates large sums to charity and works personally for the welfare of others is called?
items.explanation: A philanthropist both donates large sums and works for others' welfare. A miser is the opposite, a volunteer works without necessarily donating, and a sponsor funds without necessarily working personally.

items.question: Arrange the following sentences in a logical order. A. The bank's bad loans, however, fell by a third in the first year of the rule. B. Approvals slowed sharply, and branch managers complained that targets were being missed. C. The episode showed that a check which costs time can still pay for itself through fewer defaults. D. A bank introduced a rule that loan officers must visit every borrower's business before approving a loan. E. Managers then accepted the slower pace, and the rule was extended to larger loans as well. Choose the correct order.
items.explanation: The correct order is DBAEC: A bank introduced a rule that loan... / Approvals slowed sharply, and branch managers complained... / The bank's bad loans, however, fell by... / Managers then accepted the slower pace, and... / The episode showed that a check which... Every other option places a consequence before its cause or a reply before the statement it answers, breaking one of these links.

items.question: Arrange the following sentences in a logical order. A. The startup's app let users order groceries in ten minutes, and orders doubled every month. B. It raised delivery fees and dropped the slowest items, which slowed growth but restored the margin. C. Investors who had funded growth at any cost now asked for a plan that showed a path to profit. D. The cost of running so many small stores, however, began to eat the margin on every order. E. To keep up, it opened small dark stores in every neighbourhood, each stocked with the fastest-selling items. Choose the correct order.
items.explanation: The correct order is AEDBC: The startup's app let users order groceries... / To keep up, it opened small dark... / The cost of running so many small... / It raised delivery fees and dropped the... / Investors who had funded growth at any... Every other option places a consequence before its cause or a reply before the statement it answers, breaking one of these links.

items.question: Arrange the following sentences in a logical order. A. Errors fell sharply, and the same surgeons who had resisted began to demand the checklist in every theatre. B. The change worked not because the list was clever, but because it made the whole team speak up. C. Senior surgeons resisted it, calling it an insult to their experience. D. The hospital made the checklist a team exercise, with the youngest member reading it aloud. E. A hospital introduced a checklist for every surgery, copied from the aviation industry. Choose the correct order.
items.explanation: The correct order is ECDAB: A hospital introduced a checklist for every... / Senior surgeons resisted it, calling it an... / The hospital made the checklist a team... / Errors fell sharply, and the same surgeons... / The change worked not because the list... Every other option places a consequence before its cause or a reply before the statement it answers, breaking one of these links.

items.question: Two articles both cost Rs 500. Article A is first increased by 40% and then decreased by 25%. Article B is first decreased by 25% and then increased by 40%. By how much does the dearer article exceed the cheaper one?
items.explanation: Article A ends at Rs 500 x 1.4 x 0.75 = Rs 525, and article B ends at Rs 500 x 0.75 x 1.4 = Rs 525. Multiplication does not depend on the order, so both end at the same price and neither exceeds the other by anything. The other options come from applying only part of the two changes, which is not the difference between the two articles.

items.question: A number is first increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%, and the result is 480. What was the original number?
items.explanation: Working backwards, before the decrease the number was 480 x 100/80 = 600, and before the increase it was that value x 100/120 = 500. The other options stop after one step or treat the final value as the original, which ignores one of the two changes.

items.question: An article costs Rs 1200. It is marked up by 25%, then sold at a discount of 20% on the marked price, and then 5% tax is charged on the selling price. How much does the customer finally pay?
items.explanation: The marked price is Rs 1500. After the 20% discount the selling price is Rs 1200. Tax of 5% on that is Rs 60, so the customer pays Rs 1260. The other options stop at the marked price or the pre-tax price, which misses one of the three stages.

items.question: Class A has 40 students with average score 40 (scores range from 38 to 42). Class B has 50 students with average score 50 (scores range from 46 to 54). If 10 students are transferred from class B to class A, what is the maximum possible average score of class A after the transfer?
items.explanation: To maximise the new average, transfer the highest-scoring students from B, each scoring 54. The new total is 40 x 40 + 10 x 54 = 2140 over 50 students, giving 214/5. Transferring average or lowest scorers gives a lower average, and the old average ignores the transfer entirely, so those options are wrong.

items.question: What is the difference between the compound interest and the simple interest on Rs 15000 at 20% per annum in the first year and 10% per annum in the second year?
items.explanation: The compound interest is Rs 15000 x 1.2 x 1.1 - Rs 15000 = Rs 4800, and the simple interest is Rs 15000 x 30% = Rs 4500. The difference is Rs 4800 - Rs 4500 = Rs 300. The usual two-year formula does not apply because the rate changes, so each year must be worked out separately.

items.question: A pump can both fill and empty a tank of 3000 cubic metres. Its emptying rate is 10 cubic metres per minute higher than its filling rate, and it needs 10 minutes less to empty the tank than to fill it. What is the filling rate of the pump, in cubic metres per minute?
items.explanation: Let the filling rate be x. Then 3000/x - 3000/(x + 10) = 10, which simplifies to x squared + 10x - 3000 = 0, giving x = 50 (the negative root is rejected). The emptying rate 60 is the most tempting wrong answer, and dividing the volume by the time difference ignores the rate difference entirely.

items.question: Two numbers are in the ratio 5:3. If 8 is added to each number, the ratio becomes 3:2. What is the second number?
items.explanation: Let the numbers be 5k and 3k. Then (5k + 8)/(3k + 8) = 3/2, which gives k = 8, so the numbers are 40 and 24. The second number is 24. The other options add 8 to a number without solving for k, which confuses the changed value with the original.

items.question: The average of 6 numbers is 40. One of the numbers, 25, is replaced by 55, and then another number, 35, is replaced by 65. What is the new average?
items.explanation: The total rises by 55 - 25 = 30 at the first replacement and by 65 - 35 = 30 at the second, so it rises by 60 in all. The average rises by 60/6 = 10, giving 40 + 10 = 50. Stopping after one replacement or adding the whole rise to the average both miss a step.

items.question: A, B and C can alone complete a work in 20, 30 and 60 days respectively. They work together for 4 days, after which A leaves. In how many more days will B and C together finish the remaining work?
items.explanation: Take the total work as 60 units. A, B and C do 3, 2 and 1 units a day, so in 4 days they complete 24 units, leaving 36. B and C together do 3 units a day, so they need 36/3 = 12 more days. The other options divide the remaining work by the wrong combined rate or ignore that A has left.

items.question: A car travels 180 km at 60 km/h, then halts for 2 hour(s), then travels 120 km at 40 km/h, then travels 120 km at 60 km/h. What is the average speed of the car for the whole journey, in km/h?
items.explanation: The travelling time is 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 hours, plus a 2-hour halt, so the total time is 10 hours for 420 km. The average speed is 420/10 = 42 km/h. Ignoring the halt or averaging the three speeds directly both give wrong answers, because the legs take different times.

items.question: A train crosses a platform 100 m long in 20 seconds and a platform 200 m long in 30 seconds. What is the length of the train, in metres?
items.explanation: The train covers 100 m more in 10 seconds, so its speed is 100/10 = 10 m/s, which is 36 km/h. In 20 seconds it covers 10 x 20 = 200 m, which is the train plus the first platform, so the train is 200 - 100 = 100 m long. A single platform and time cannot fix the length, because the speed is unknown.

items.question: 30 litres of a solution with 25% acid is mixed with 20 litres of a solution with 55% acid. How many litres of pure acid must be added to make the acid concentration of the resulting mixture 50%?
items.explanation: The mixture has 18.5 litres of acid in 50 litres. Adding 13 litres of pure acid gives 18.5 + 13 = 31.5 litres of acid in 50 + 13 = 63 litres, which is 50%. Simply adding the shortfall of 6.5 litres ignores that the added acid also increases the total volume.

items.question: The marked price of an article is Rs 1600. A shop offers two successive discounts of 25% and 10%, while another shop offers a single discount of 30%. By how much is the cheaper of the two offers cheaper than the other?
items.explanation: The successive discounts give Rs 1080 and the single discount gives Rs 1120, so the successive discounts is cheaper by Rs 40. The other options give one of the selling prices or only the first discount, which does not compare the two offers.

items.question: What is the smallest number greater than 250 which, when divided by 4 and by 9, leaves a remainder of 2 in each case?
items.explanation: A number leaving remainder 2 on division by both 4 and 9 is 2 more than a multiple of their LCM, 36. The multiples of 36 near 250 are 216 and 252, and 252 + 2 = 254 is the first value above 250. The other options are the previous or next such number, or simply 250 + 2, which is not a multiple of 36 plus 2.

items.question: In a factory, machine A produces 60% with 5% defective, machine B produces 25% with 10% defective, machine C produces 15% with 10% defective. A toy drawn at random is found to be defective. What is the probability that it was made on machine A? Give your answer as a fraction.
items.explanation: The total defective probability is the weighted sum 7/100, and machine A contributes 3/100 of it, so the required probability is 3/100/7/100 = 3/7. The machine's share of output and its defect rate are both tempting wrong answers, because each ignores the other factor and the base rate.

items.question: What is the smallest number which, when divided by 6, leaves a remainder of 4 and when divided by 7, leaves a remainder of 5?
items.explanation: Numbers leaving remainder 4 on division by 6 are 4, 10, 16, and so on. The first of them that also leaves remainder 5 on division by 7 is 40: 40 = 6 x 6 + 4 and 40 = 7 x 5 + 5. Adding the LCM to the remainder, or using the LCM alone, gives a number with the wrong remainders.

items.question: Let n be the smallest positive integer greater than 60 that is divisible by 11 and leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 4. What is the unit digit of 3 raised to the power n plus 7 raised to the power n?
items.explanation: First find n. The multiples of 11 above 60 are 66 and 77. 66 leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 4, while 77 leaves a remainder of 1, so n = 77. The unit digits of powers of 3 cycle 3, 9, 7, 1 and of 7 cycle 7, 9, 3, 1, with period 4. Since 77 leaves remainder 1 on division by 4, 3^77 ends in 3 and 7^77 ends in 7, so their sum ends in 0. An exponent leaving remainder 0 on division by 4 would give 2, and remainder 2 would give 8.

items.question: A quadratic equation x squared + bx + 44 = 0 has two positive roots. The sum of the squares of the roots is 137. What is the larger root?
items.explanation: Let the roots be a and b. Then ab = 44 and a squared + b squared = 137, so (a + b) squared = 137 + 2 x 44 = 225, giving a + b = 15, since both roots are positive. So a and b are the roots of t squared - 15t + 44 = 0, which factors as (t - 11)(t - 4) = 0. The roots are 11 and 4, so the larger root is 11. 15 is the sum of the roots, 4 is the smaller root, and 44 is their product.

items.question: A is 3 times as old as B. In 5 years, A will be 2 times as old as B. What is A's present age, in years?
items.explanation: Let B's present age be x. Then A is 3x, and in 5 years 3x + 5 = 2(x + 5), which gives x = 5, so A is 3 x 5 = 15 years old. The other options give B's age, A's age in 5 years, or the sum of the two ages.

items.question: The equation x squared - 9x + k = 0 has two roots, one of which is twice the other. What is the value of k?
items.explanation: Let the roots be y and 2y. Their sum is 3y = 9, so y = 3 and the roots are 3 and 6. Their product is k = 3 x 6 = 18. The other options confuse the product with the square of one root or with the sum of the roots.

items.question: Three positive integers a, b, c, where a <= b <= c, satisfy a + b + c = 18 and ab + bc + ca = 89. Additionally, a, b, c are pairwise coprime. What are the possible values of abc?
items.explanation: Let c be the largest. Then a + b = 18 - c and ab = 89 - c(18 - c) = c squared - 18c + 89. The discriminant of the quadratic with roots a and b is (18 - c) squared - 4(c squared - 18c + 89) = -3c squared + 36c - 32, which must be a non-negative perfect square, and the roots must not exceed c. Checking c from 6 upwards: c = 8 gives discriminant 64, but its roots are 1 and 9, and 9 exceeds c, so it is the same triple as the c = 9 case, not a new one. c = 9 gives discriminant 49 and roots 1 and 8, so (1, 8, 9) with abc = 72; c = 11 gives discriminant 1 and roots 3 and 4, so (3, 4, 11) with abc = 132. No other c gives a perfect square with roots not exceeding c, and both triples are pairwise coprime, so the possible products are 72 and 132.

items.question: The ratio of the present ages of A and B is 9:7. After 8 years, the ratio of their ages will become 5:4. What is A's present age?
items.explanation: Let the ages be 9k and 7k. Then (9k + 8)/(7k + 8) = 5/4, which gives k = 8, so A is 9 x 8 = 72 years old. The other options give B's age, A's age after 8 years, or a value obtained by adding 8 to the ratio instead of to the ages.

items.question: The sum of the ages of A and B is 32 years, the sum of the ages of B and C is 23 years, and the sum of the ages of A and C is 27 years. What is B's age?
items.explanation: Adding all three sums gives twice the sum of the three ages, so A + B + C = 41. Subtracting the sum of A and C, 27, gives B = 41 - 27 = 14 years. The other options give A's age, C's age, or the total of the three ages.

items.question: A rectangle has perimeter 52 m and its length is 8 m more than its breadth. What is the area of the rectangle, in square metres?
items.explanation: Length plus breadth is 52/2 = 26 m, and length minus breadth is 8 m, so the length is 17 m and the breadth is 9 m. The area is 17 x 9 = 153 square metres. The other options square the length, multiply the perimeter by the breadth, or add an arbitrary amount.

items.question: A circle is inscribed in a square. If the radius of the circle is increased by 30%, by what percentage does the area of the region inside the square but outside the circle increase?
items.explanation: With radius r, the square has area 4r squared and the circle has area pi r squared, so the region between them has area (4 - pi) r squared. Increasing r by 30% multiplies every area by (1 + 30/100) squared = 1.69, so the region also grows by 69%. The region scales with the square of the radius, just as the circle does, so doubling the percentage or using the percentage once both miss the square.

items.question: A cuboid has length 2 cm, volume 60 cubic cm and total surface area 112 square cm. What is the larger of its other two dimensions, in cm?
items.explanation: The product of the other two dimensions is 60/2 = 30, and from the surface area their sum is 13. Two numbers with sum 13 and product 30 are 3 and 10, so the larger is 10 cm. The other options give the smaller dimension, the sum, or the product.

items.question: In how many ways can 4 people be arranged in a row if 2 particular people must always sit together, and a third particular person must not sit next to either of them?
items.explanation: With the two together as one block there are 2 x 3! = 12 arrangements, but some of them put the third person next to the block. Removing the arrangements where the third person sits immediately beside the block leaves 4. Arranging all 4 freely ignores the together condition, and counting the block alone ignores the exclusion.

items.question: A bag has 6 red balls and 4 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random, one after another, without replacement. Given that at least one ball is red, what is the probability that both balls are red? Give your answer as a fraction.
items.explanation: The condition changes the sample space: pairs with at least one red number C(10,2) - C(4,2) = 45 - 6 = 39. Both red pairs number C(6,2) = 15, so the probability is 15/39 = 5/13. Using the unconditional sample space, or the probability of one red draw, both ignore the condition.

items.question: Two fair dice are thrown together. Given that at least one die shows an even number, what is the probability that the sum of the numbers shown is 11? Give your answer as a fraction.
items.explanation: The condition leaves 27 equally likely outcomes, those with at least one even number. Of these, 2 add to 11, so the probability is 2/27 = 2/27. Using all 36 outcomes ignores the condition, and counting only the pairs that add to 11 without checking the condition overcounts.

items.question: In a group of 150 students, 25 do only chess, 20 do only badminton, 15 do only swimming, 30 do exactly two of the three activities, and 10 do all three. How many students do none of the three activities?
items.explanation: The students doing at least one activity are 25 + 20 + 15 + 30 + 10 = 100, since the only, exactly-two and all-three groups do not overlap. Subtracting from 150 gives 50 who do none. The other options forget the exactly-two group or the all-three group when adding up.

items.question: Using the Patients admitted in four wards, 2021 to 2024 table, if the year in which W was lowest is removed from the table, what is the ratio of W's total to Y's total over the remaining years?

diagram.caption: Patients admitted in four wards, 2021 to 2024

items.explanation: W was lowest in 2021, at 55, so 2021 is removed. Over 2022 to 2024, W totals 70 + 80 + 95 = 245 and Y totals 25 + 25 + 20 = 70, and 245 : 70 simplifies to 7 : 2. Using the full four years gives 300 : 100, or 3 : 1, which is the trap for solvers who skip the removal step.

items.question: In the Patients admitted in four wards, 2021 to 2024 table, for X, in which year was the year-on-year growth rate the highest?
items.explanation: The growth rates for X are 25/2% in 2022, 200/9% in 2023, 100/11% in 2024. The highest is in 2023. Comparing raw values instead of rates would pick a later year, which is the trap this question sets.

items.question: In the Patients admitted in four wards, 2021 to 2024 table, in which year was W's share of that year's total across all columns the highest?
items.explanation: W's shares are 1100/43% in 2021, 700/23% in 2022, 1600/51% in 2023, 95/3% in 2024. The highest share is in 2024. The raw value of W rises every year, so a reader who compares raw values instead of shares picks the wrong year.

items.question: Which column of the Patients admitted in four wards, 2021 to 2024 table fell by the largest percentage between 2021 and 2024?
items.explanation: The percentage changes from 2021 to 2024 are W: 800/11%, X: 50%, Y: -100/3%, Z: 30%. The largest fall is Y at 100/3%. A column with a large absolute fall can have a small percentage fall, so the raw difference is not the answer.

items.question: In the Patients admitted in four wards, 2021 to 2024 table, which of the following statements must be true?
options: W exceeded X in every year.
items.explanation: X rose in every year: 80, then 90, then 110, then 120, so the fourth statement is true. W did not exceed X in any year: W was 55, 70, 80 and 95 against X at 80, 90, 110 and 120. Y did not fall every year: it was 25 in both 2022 and 2023. The total of Z is 200 while the total of W is 300, so Z does not exceed W.

items.question: Using the bar chart of Sales (in Rs lakh) in five regions, which category has the largest combined total across 2023 and 2024?

diagram.caption: Sales (in Rs lakh) in five regions (2023 vs 2024)

items.explanation: The combined totals are North: 500, South: 275, West: 530, East: 320, Central: 175. The largest is West with 530. A category that leads in one year need not lead in the combined total, so each year's leader must be checked against the sum.

items.question: In the bar chart of Sales (in Rs lakh) in five regions, if the category with the smallest 2023 value is excluded, by how much did the total rise from 2023 to 2024 across the remaining categories?
items.explanation: The smallest 2023 value is Central, at 75, so Central is excluded. The 2023 total across the remaining regions is 800 minus 75 = 725, and the 2024 total across them is 1,000 minus 100 = 900, so the rise is 900 minus 725 = 175. The full rise of 200 ignores the exclusion, 150 is the rise if the largest category is excluded instead, and 25 is Central's own rise.

items.question: In the bar chart of Sales (in Rs lakh) in five regions, in which category is the absolute difference between the 2024 value and the 2023 value the largest?
items.explanation: The differences are North: 60, South: 25, West: 50, East: 40, Central: 25. The largest is North with 60. The category with the highest percentage growth is not necessarily the one with the largest absolute difference, since the bases differ.

items.question: In the bar chart of Sales (in Rs lakh) in five regions, the 2024 value for East is smudged and cannot be read. The average of the three largest 2024 values across the five categories is 250. What is the 2024 value for East?
items.explanation: The readable 2024 values are West 290, North 280, South 150 and Central 100. Let East's value be c. The three largest values must average 250, so they sum to 750. If c were below 180, the three largest would be 290, 280 and 150, averaging 240, which contradicts 250. If c were 180 or more, the three largest would be 290, 280 and c, so c = 750 - 290 - 280 = 180, which is consistent. So East's 2024 value is 180. 250 is the stated average, not the missing value, and 150 is the next readable value.

items.question: In the bar chart of Sales (in Rs lakh) in five regions, which category grew by the highest percentage from 2023 to 2024?
items.explanation: The growth rates are North: 300/11%, South: 20%, West: 125/6%, East: 200/7%, Central: 100/3%. The highest is Central. The largest absolute increase belongs to a different category, which is why the percentage, not the raw increase, decides this question.

items.passage: The two pie charts show how investment portfolio was divided in 2023 and 2024. In 2023 the shares were Equity 50%, Debt 25%, Gold 10%, Real estate 10%, Cash 5%, on a total of Rs 40000. The 2024 shares are shown in the pie chart, on a total of Rs 60000.
items.question: The 2023 shares were Equity 50%, Debt 25%, Gold 10%, Real estate 10%, Cash 5%, on a total of Rs 40,000. The 2024 shares are shown in the pie chart, on a total of Rs 60,000. In the Investment portfolio pie charts, by how much did the amount spent on Equity change from 2023 to 2024?
items.explanation: The amount on Equity in 2023 was 50% of Rs 40000, which is Rs 20000, and in 2024 it was 58% of Rs 60000, which is Rs 34800. The change is Rs 34800 - Rs 20000 = Rs 14800, an increase. The change must be worked out from each year's own share and total; working from one year's total alone, or from the shares alone, gives the wrong change.

items.question: The 2023 shares were Equity 50%, Debt 25%, Gold 10%, Real estate 10%, Cash 5%, on a total of Rs 40,000. The 2024 shares are shown in the pie chart, on a total of Rs 60,000. In the Investment portfolio pie charts, comparing the 2023 and 2024 shares, which category's share rose by the most percentage points?
items.explanation: The changes in percentage points are Equity: +8, Debt: -5, Gold: +5, Real estate: -5, Cash: -3. The largest rise is Equity. A category whose amount rose may still have lost share, so the share change, not the amount change, decides this question.

items.question: The 2023 shares were Equity 50%, Debt 25%, Gold 10%, Real estate 10%, Cash 5%, on a total of Rs 40,000. The 2024 shares are shown in the pie chart, on a total of Rs 60,000. In the Investment portfolio pie charts, by how much did the combined amount spent on Debt and Gold increase from 2023 to 2024?
items.explanation: In 2023 the two categories together were 35% of Rs 40000, which is Rs 14000, and in 2024 they were 35% of Rs 60000, which is Rs 21000. The increase is Rs 21000 - Rs 14000 = Rs 7000. Either year's combined amount alone is not the increase, and the change in share alone does not give it either, because the total also changed.

items.question: The 2023 shares were Equity 50%, Debt 25%, Gold 10%, Real estate 10%, Cash 5%, on a total of Rs 40,000. The 2024 shares are shown in the pie chart, on a total of Rs 60,000. In the Investment portfolio pie charts, in 2024 the amount spent on Cash is what percentage of the amount spent on Equity in 2023?
items.explanation: The amount on Cash in 2024 is 2% of Rs 60000, which is Rs 1200, and the amount on Equity in 2023 is 50% of Rs 40000, which is Rs 20000. The ratio is 1200/20000 = 6%. A same-year ratio, a ratio of the shares, or the reciprocal all give wrong answers, because each amount must come from its own year's share and total.

items.question: The 2023 shares were Equity 50%, Debt 25%, Gold 10%, Real estate 10%, Cash 5%, on a total of Rs 40,000. The 2024 shares are shown in the pie chart, on a total of Rs 60,000. In the Investment portfolio pie charts, the amount spent on Equity in 2024 is what percentage of the amount spent on Debt in 2023?
items.explanation: Equity in 2024 is 58% of Rs 60000, which is Rs 34800, and Debt in 2023 is 25% of Rs 40000, which is Rs 10000. The ratio is 34800/10000 = 348%. Both amounts must be derived from their own year's share and total before the ratio can be formed, which is why same-year ratios are wrong.

items.question: What is the value of a? I. a squared - 9a + 20 = 0. II. a is greater than 4.
items.explanation: Statement I alone gives a = 4 or a = 5, since a squared - 9a + 20 factors as (a - 4)(a - 5) = 0, so it does not fix a. Statement II alone leaves a unbounded. Together, only a = 5 satisfies both, so both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is sufficient.

items.question: Is the triangle right-angled? I. Two sides are 20 and 21 cm. II. The third side is 29 cm.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone gives all three sides. Together, 20 squared plus 21 squared is 841, which equals 29 squared, so by Pythagoras the triangle is right-angled. The verdict depends on the hidden fact of Pythagoras, not on either statement alone.

items.question: Is n divisible by 12? I. n is divisible by 4. II. n is divisible by 15.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone implies divisibility by 12. Together, since 4 and 15 are coprime, n is divisible by their product 60, which is a multiple of 12. The coprimality is the hidden fact that makes the two statements jointly sufficient.

items.question: Is x greater than y? I. x + y = 40. II. x - y = 16.
items.explanation: Statement I alone does not settle it: x = 28 and y = 12 satisfy x + y = 40 with x greater than y, while x = 12 and y = 28 also satisfy it with x less than y. Statement II alone gives x - y = 16, which is positive, so x is greater than y. So Statement II alone is sufficient. The two equations together would find x and y, but they are not needed to answer the question.

items.question: What is the speed of the stream? I. The boat speed in still water is 18 km/h. II. The downstream speed is 25 km/h.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone gives the stream speed. Together, the stream speed is downstream minus still-water speed, 25 - 18 = 7 km/h. Both statements together are needed, and neither alone is enough.

items.question: What is the HCF of the two numbers? I. Their product is 660. II. Their LCM is 110.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone gives the HCF. Together, the product of two numbers equals their HCF times their LCM, so the HCF is 660/110 = 6. The product-LCM identity is the hidden fact that makes the two statements jointly sufficient.

items.question: What is the new average of 6 numbers after one number is replaced? I. The old average is 40. II. The number 25 is replaced by 55.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone gives the new average. Together, the total rises by 30, so the average rises by 30/6 = 5, giving 45. Both statements together are needed, and neither alone is enough.

items.question: What is the profit percentage on the article? I. The cost price is Rs 1000. II. The marked price is Rs 1500 and the discount is 20%.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone gives the profit. Together, the selling price is Rs 1500 less 20%, which is Rs 1200, so the profit is Rs 200 on Rs 1000, which is 20%. Both statements together are needed, and neither alone is enough.

items.question: What is A's age? I. The ratio of the ages of A and B is 4:3. II. The sum of their ages is 56 years.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone gives A's age. Together, A is 4/7 of the total 56, which is 32 years. Both statements together are needed, and neither alone is enough.

items.question: Is a greater than 0? I. a squared is 25. II. a is not negative.
items.explanation: Statement I alone leaves a as 5 or -5. Statement II alone does not fix a value. Together, a is 5, which is greater than 0. Both together are needed. The other options claim a different statement is enough, which does not follow from the given facts.

items.question: In how many days can A alone complete the work? I. A and B together can complete it in 12 days. II. B alone can complete it in 20 days.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone gives A's time. Together, A does 1/12 - 1/20 = 8/240 of the work per day, so A alone takes 30 days. Both statements together are needed, and neither alone is enough.

items.question: What is the two-digit number? I. It leaves a remainder of 2 when divided by 7. II. It is a multiple of 9.
items.explanation: Neither statement alone fixes the number. Together, the two-digit multiples of 9 with remainder 2 on division by 7 leave only 72. The uniqueness comes from checking the whole range, which is the hidden step that makes the two statements jointly sufficient.

items.passage: In a survey, 250 customers use apps for shopping, food and travel. 24% of them do only shopping, 20% do only food and 16% do only travel. 25 do exactly shopping and food, 20 do exactly food and travel, 15 do exactly shopping and travel, and 40 do all three. Of those who do only shopping, one-half are female; of those who do only food, three-fifths are female; of those who do only travel, three-fourths are female; of those who do exactly shopping and food, two-fifths are female; of those who do exactly food and travel, one-fourth are female; of those who do exactly shopping and travel, one-third are female; and of those who do all three, one-fourth are female.
items.question: In the survey described, how many females do exactly two activities?
items.explanation: Exactly two activities means shopping and food, food and travel, or shopping and travel. The females in those groups are 25 x 2/5 = 10, 20 x 1/4 = 5 and 15 x 1/3 = 5, a total of 20.

items.question: How many of the 250 customers are female?
items.explanation: The female counts by region are 30, 30, 30, 10, 5, 5, 10, which add to 120. Each region's female count must be worked out from its own fraction before adding, because the fractions differ by region. The other options miss one region or use the male total instead.

items.question: The number of males who do all three (shopping, food and travel) is what percentage of the total number of females?
items.explanation: There are 40 who do all three, of whom 10 are female, so 30 are male. The total number of females is 120, so the required percentage is 30/120 = 25%. Both the numerator and the denominator are themselves derived quantities, and using the all-three total or the grand total as the base gives the wrong options.

items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Blood Relations
items.question: M is the wife of N. N is the brother of O. O is the father of P. P is the wife of Q. How is M related to Q?
items.explanation: O is the father of P, and N is O's brother, so N is P's uncle and M, N's wife, is P's aunt. P is the wife of Q, so M is the wife of the brother of Q's father-in-law, which makes M Q's aunt-in-law.

items.question: X is the son of Y. Y is the brother of Z. Z is the mother of W. How is X related to W?
items.explanation: Y is Z's brother and Z is W's mother, so Y is W's maternal uncle. X is Y's son, so X is W's cousin. X is not W's brother, since they have different parents, and X is Z's nephew, not W's.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Blood Relations

items.question: A is the mother of B and C. B is the wife of D. D is the brother of E. How is A related to E?
items.explanation: B is D's wife, so B is the sister-in-law of D's sibling E. A is B's mother, so A is the mother of E's sister-in-law. A is not E's mother-in-law, since E's spouse is not in the chain, and A is neither E's aunt nor E's sister.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Blood Relations

items.question: X is the mother of Y and Z. Y is married to W. W is the father of V. Z is unmarried. Which of the following is true?
options: Z is the aunt of V
W is the daughter of X
V is the niece of Z
V is the grandchild of X
items.explanation: Y is married to W and W is the father of V, so V is Y's child. X is Y's mother, so V is X's grandchild. Z's gender is not given, so Z may be V's aunt or uncle; W is Y's spouse, X's son-in-law, not X's daughter; and V's gender is not given, so V may be Z's niece or nephew.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Blood Relations

items.question: In a certain code, each letter of a word is moved forward in the alphabet by its position in the word: the first letter by 1 place, the second by 2 places, and so on. For example, COLD is coded as DQOH. How is KING coded under the same rule?
items.explanation: Work out the rule from the example: in COLD, the first letter moves 1 place, the second 2 places, the third 3 places and the fourth 4 places, giving DQOH. Apply the same shifts to KING: K moves 1 place to L, I moves 2 places to K, N moves 3 places to Q and G moves 4 places to K, giving LKQK. The LKOH option comes from shifting vowels by 2 and consonants by 1, the reversed word comes from reversing without shifting, and the LKQJ option differs from the correct code in the final letter only.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Coding Decoding

items.question: In a certain code, a word is first reversed. Then the first letter of the reversed word is moved 1 place forward, and each later letter is moved 2 places forward if the letter before it is a vowel, and 1 place back if the letter before it is a consonant. Two examples are given: JUMP is coded as QLTL, and GAME is coded as FOZI. How is ROAD coded under the same rule?
items.explanation: First find the rule from the examples: each coded letter depends on the letter before it, so the rule has to be worked out letter by letter rather than applied uniformly. For ROAD, reverse it to get DAOR. Then D moves 1 place forward to E; A moves 1 place back to Z because the letter before it, D, is a consonant; O moves 2 places forward to Q because the letter before it, A, is a vowel; R moves 2 places forward to T because the letter before it, O, is a vowel, giving EZQT. The FCQT option reverses and shifts every letter by 2, the SNCF option applies the chain without reversing, and the reversed word alone ignores the shifts.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Coding Decoding

items.question: In a code, a word is written as two numbers: the sum of the alphabet positions of its 1st and 3rd letters, followed by the sum of the positions of its 2nd and 4th letters. If COLD is coded as 1519, how is ROAD coded under the same rule?
items.explanation: For ROAD, the 1st and 3rd letters sum to 19 and the 2nd and 4th sum to 19, giving 1919. The total of all four positions, or the two sums in the wrong order, are the traps.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Coding Decoding

items.question: In a certain code, each letter of a word is shifted by the next letter in the word: a letter moves 2 places forward if the next letter is a vowel, and 1 place back if the next letter is a consonant. The last letter moves 1 place forward. Two examples are given: TRAIN is coded as STCHO, and SPARE is coded as RRZTF. Using the same code, the coded form ONZMU stands for which word?
items.explanation: Work out the rule from the examples: in TRAIN, each letter's shift depends on the letter after it, so a letter before a vowel moves 2 places forward and a letter before a consonant moves 1 place back, with the last letter moving 1 place forward. Test the options against the code ONZMU: PLANT gives ONZMU; PLANE gives ONZPF; PLANK gives ONZML; PLANS gives ONZMT. Only PLANT matches exactly, and each other option differs in exactly one coded letter, so the rule has to be applied to the whole word rather than guessed from a single letter.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Coding Decoding

items.question: What is the next number in the series: 7, 9, 10, 15, 13, 21, ?
items.explanation: The terms in odd positions rise by 3 and the terms in even positions rise by 6, so the next term, in an odd position, is the last odd term plus 3, which is 16. Continuing one step too far, or one step short, gives the other options.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Number Series

items.question: What is the next number in the series: 3, 7, 15, 27, 43, 63, ?
items.explanation: The differences between consecutive terms are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, which themselves rise by 4 each time. The next difference is 24, so the next term is 63 + 24 = 87. Using a constant difference or the wrong step gives the other options.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Number Series

items.question: What is the next number in the series: 2, 6, 7, 21, 22, 66, ?
items.explanation: The operations repeat in a cycle of two: multiply by 3, then add 1. So 2 x 3 = 6, 6 + 1 = 7, 7 x 3 = 21, 21 + 1 = 22, 22 x 3 = 66, and the next operation is add 1, giving 67.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Number Series

items.question: What is the next letter in the series: D, F, I, M, R, ?
items.explanation: The steps grow by one each time: +2, +3, +4, +5, so the next step is +6, giving X. A fixed step of +2, or continuing the last step of +5, or one step too far, give the other options.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Letter Series

items.question: What is the next letter in the series: B, E, E, G, H, I, ?
items.explanation: The letters in odd positions advance by 3 places and those in even positions advance by 2 places, wrapping from Z back to A. The next term is in an odd position, so it is the last odd letter advanced by 3, which is K. Letters one step either side, or the result of the wrong progression, are the traps.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Letter Series

items.question: Statements: All dogs are animals. No animal is a plant. Some pets are dogs. Conclusions: I. No pet is a plant. II. Some pets are animals. Which of the conclusions follow?
options: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow
items.explanation: Some pets are dogs and all dogs are animals, so some pets are animals. Only some pets are dogs, so other pets could be plants, and the first conclusion does not follow. The other verdicts claim a conclusion that the premises do not support, or deny one that they do support.

items.question: Statements: Some M are N. All N are O. Some O are P. Which of the following statements is definitely true?
items.explanation: Some M are N and all N are O, so some M are O. The P group is only some of O, so M need not reach it, and no M being P does not follow either. The other statements are either false under the premises or true only in some cases, not in all cases.

items.question: Statements: Some dogs are pets. All pets are animals. Conclusions: I. Some dogs are animals. II. All dogs are animals. Which of the conclusions follow?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
items.explanation: Some dogs are pets and all pets are animals, so some dogs are animals. Only some dogs are pets, so all dogs being animals does not follow. The other verdicts claim a conclusion that the premises do not support, or deny one that they do support.

items.question: In a group of 200 members of a society, 40 do only reading, 35 do only music and 30 do only sports. The number who do exactly two of the three is twice the number who do all three, and 45 do at least two of the three. How many do none of the three?
items.explanation: Let the number who do all three be x. Then exactly two is 2x, and at least two is 2x + x = 3x = 45, so x = 15 and exactly two is 30. Everyone is accounted for by only-one (40 + 35 + 30 = 105), exactly-two (30), all-three (15) and none, so none = 200 - 105 - 30 - 15 = 50. Using the exactly-two count, or the all-three count, or adding the all-three count to the answer, gives the other options.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Venn Diagram

items.question: Among the 180 members of a society, 35 do only reading, 30 do only music and 25 do only sports, and 48 do none of the three. 12 members do all three of reading, music and sports. How many do exactly two of reading, music and sports?
items.explanation: The members doing only one activity number 35 + 30 + 25 = 90, and 48 do none, so those doing at least two number 180 - 90 - 48 = 42. Of these, 12 do all three, so those doing exactly two number 42 - 12 = 30. The at-least-two total 42 and the all-three count 12 are the traps.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Venn Diagram

items.question: Among the 180 members of a society, 35 do only reading, 30 do only music and 25 do only sports. 30 members do exactly two of reading, music and sports, and 12 do all three. How many do none of reading, music and sports?
items.explanation: Those doing at least one activity number 35 + 30 + 25 + 30 + 12 = 132, so those doing none number 180 - 132 = 48. Forgetting the exactly-two group or the all-three group when adding up gives the wrong options.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Venn Diagram

items.passage: 6 people sit in a row from left to right. (1) O sits at the left end. (2) M sits second from the right end. (3) N sits immediately to the left of M. (4) P sits between O and N. (5) Q sits immediately to the right of P. (6) R sits at the right end. Use the clues to work out the arrangement.
items.question: Who sits at the left end of the row of M, N, O, P, Q and R?
items.explanation: Combining the clues gives the unique order O, P, Q, N, M, R from left to right, so the left end is O. The other people sit elsewhere in the row, and no clue alone gives the answer.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Seating Arrangement

items.question: Using the same arrangement, who sits between P and N?
items.explanation: In the solved order O, P, Q, N, M, R, Q sits between P and N. The answer needs the full arrangement, since no single clue places Q between those two.
items.topic: Intelligence and Critical Reasoning - Seating Arrangement

items.question: In the arrangement of M, N, O, P, Q and R, which of the following statements is definitely true?
options: M sits at the left end
O sits at the right end
R sits at the right end
items.explanation: In the solved order O, P, Q, N, M, R, the statement 'R sits at the right end' holds, while each of the other statements contradicts the solved order. Only the complete solution settles this question.

items.question: A diet app's users lose weight, and the company claims the app causes weight loss. Which of the following most strengthens the claim?
options: Users given the app lost more weight than a matched group without it, while eating the same diet.
The app is popular with users.
Weight loss takes a long time.
items.explanation: A matched comparison that holds diet constant isolates the app's effect, which is what the claim needs. The other options praise the app without testing whether it causes the loss.

items.question: A city banned plastic bags and litter fell. The council claims the ban reduced litter. Which of the following most weakens the claim?
options: The city also doubled street cleaning in the same months.
Plastic bags are harmful to the environment.
items.explanation: Doubled street cleaning is a rival explanation for less litter, so the ban may not be the cause. The other options support the ban or describe its effects without offering a rival cause.

items.question: A new metro line opens and bus ridership falls. The operator claims passengers switched to the metro. The same month bus fares rose, and the metro offered free travel for its first month. Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the operator's claim?
options: Passengers said they preferred the metro.
Routes where the metro opened but bus fares did not rise kept their riders, while routes where fares rose lost riders whether or not the metro served them.
Bus ridership also fell in a city with no metro.
The metro is faster than the bus.
items.explanation: The claim attributes the fall to passengers switching to the metro, but bus fares rose at the same time, so the two changes are confounded. The second option separates them: where only the metro opened, riders stayed, and where only fares rose, riders left, so the fall tracks the fare rise, not the metro. Passengers preferring the metro says nothing about why they stopped taking the bus, a fall elsewhere could have a different cause, and the metro being faster does not show it caused this fall.

items.question: A firm's profits rose after it cut prices, while its rivals, who kept prices unchanged, saw profits fall. What can be inferred?
options: Rivals should cut their prices too.
The price cut may have won customers from rivals.
items.explanation: Profits rose at the firm that cut prices and fell at rivals that did not, which is consistent with customers moving. The other options state universal rules the two observations cannot prove.

items.question: Students who take private tuition score higher, so tuition causes higher scores. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Families who can afford tuition may also provide better study conditions, so tuition may not be the cause.
Scores depend on how hard students work.
items.explanation: The argument ignores that tuition takers differ from others in wealth and study conditions, which could explain the scores. The other options are facts about tuition that do not identify the error.

items.question: A man walks 12 km east and then 9 km north. He then turns and walks straight back towards his starting point, stopping halfway. How far is he from his starting point now, in km?
items.explanation: After the two legs he is 15 km from the start, the hypotenuse of a 12-9-15 triangle. Walking halfway back along the straight line leaves him 15/2 = 7.5 km away. The full distance, or half the sum of the legs, are the traps here.

items.question: A and B start at the same point. A walks 3 km east, then 4 km north, then 3 km west. B walks 10 km south. How far apart are A and B, in km?
items.explanation: A ends 4 km north of the start, since the east and west legs cancel, and B ends 10 km south of the start, so they are 4 + 10 = 14 km apart. Either single distance alone, or a value that adds the cancelled legs, is wrong.

items.question: Which of the following pairs shares the same relationship as King : Crown, where the second is worn or carried by the first as the visible sign of the first's office?
items.explanation: A crown is worn by a king as the visible sign of kingship, not merely as something a king uses. A gavel is carried by a judge as the visible sign of judicial office: it is used to call a court to order and to pronounce judgement. A gun is a soldier's weapon, a stethoscope is a doctor's diagnostic tool, and a plough is a farmer's tool; none of them is the visible sign of the person's office.

items.question: The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana was launched in 2014. The Unified Payments Interface was launched in 2016. The Goods and Services Tax was launched in 2017. Consider the following statements. (1) The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana was launched before the Unified Payments Interface. (2) The Goods and Services Tax was launched after the Unified Payments Interface. (3) All three were launched in the same decade. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 2014 comes before 2016. Statement 2 is correct: 2017 comes after 2016. Statement 3 is correct: 2014, 2016 and 2017 are all in the 2010s.

items.question: A country's exports in five years were Rs 120 crore, Rs 150 crore, Rs 180 crore, Rs 210 crore and Rs 240 crore. Consider the following statements. (1) The total exports over the five years were Rs 900 crore. (2) Exports rose every year. (3) The last year's exports were double the first year's exports. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 120 + 150 + 180 + 210 + 240 = 900. Statement 2 is correct: each year is higher than the one before it. Statement 3 is correct: 240 is double 120.

items.question: A bank's loan book is Rs 1,000 crore: home loans Rs 400 crore, personal loans Rs 250 crore, business loans Rs 200 crore and agriculture loans Rs 150 crore. Consider the following statements. (1) Home loans account for 40 percent of the loan book. (2) Personal loans exceed business loans by Rs 60 crore. (3) Agriculture loans account for 15 percent of the loan book. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 400 out of 1,000 is 40 percent. Statement 2 is incorrect: 250 minus 200 is 50, not 60. Statement 3 is correct: 150 out of 1,000 is 15 percent.

items.question: The price of petrol rises from Rs 100 per litre to Rs 110 per litre. A taxi uses 100 litres of petrol a month. Consider the following statements. (1) The price of petrol rises by 10 percent. (2) The taxi's monthly fuel cost rises by Rs 1,000. (3) The rise in the monthly fuel cost is more than the price of 10 litres at the old price. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 10 out of 100 is 10 percent. Statement 2 is correct: the monthly cost rises from Rs 10,000 to Rs 11,000. Statement 3 is incorrect: 10 litres at the old price cost Rs 1,000, which equals the rise, so the rise is not more than that amount.

items.question: Scheme A covers 60 lakh people at Rs 500 each. Scheme B covers 40 lakh people at Rs 1,000 each. Consider the following statements. (1) Scheme B costs more in total than scheme A. (2) Scheme A covers more people than scheme B. (3) Scheme A's cost per person is higher than scheme B's. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: A costs 60 lakh times 500, or Rs 300 crore, while B costs 40 lakh times 1,000, or Rs 400 crore. Statement 2 is correct: 60 lakh is more than 40 lakh. Statement 3 is incorrect: 500 is less than 1,000.

items.question: A current account deficit arises when a country's imports of goods and services exceed its exports of goods and services. A country exports Rs 400 crore and imports Rs 450 crore. Consider the following statements. (1) There is a current account deficit of Rs 50 crore. (2) Exports exceed imports. (3) The deficit is 12.5 percent of exports. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 450 minus 400 is 50, and imports exceed exports, so it is a deficit. Statement 2 is incorrect: exports of 400 are less than imports of 450. Statement 3 is correct: 50 out of 400 is 12.5 percent.

items.question: A city's bus ridership fell from June. Three explanations are offered: a fare rise in May that applied to all routes, a metro line that opened in June, and a festival that ended in April. Further facts: ridership fell only on the routes the metro serves, and other routes were unchanged. Consider the following statements. (1) The festival ending cannot explain the fall, because the fall began in June, two months after the festival ended. (2) The fare rise cannot explain the fall, because it applied to all routes but the fall is only on the routes the metro serves. (3) The metro opening is supported as a cause, because the fall matches it in place and in timing. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: an April event cannot cause a fall that began in June. Statement 2 is correct: a fare rise on all routes cannot explain a fall on some routes only. Statement 3 is correct: the fall is confined to the routes the metro serves and began when it opened.

items.question: A factory must keep its debt below 50 percent of its capital. Its capital is Rs 200 crore and its debt is Rs 90 crore. Consider the following statements. (1) The debt limit is Rs 100 crore. (2) The factory is within the limit. (3) The factory's debt ratio is 45 percent. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 50 percent of 200 is 100. Statement 2 is correct: 90 is less than 100. Statement 3 is correct: 90 out of 200 is 45 percent.

items.question: A bank's deposits were Rs 1,000 crore in 2021, Rs 1,100 crore in 2022, Rs 1,210 crore in 2023 and Rs 1,331 crore in 2024. Consider the following statements. (1) Deposits grew by 10 percent every year. (2) Total growth from 2021 to 2024 was 33.1 percent. (3) The 2024 value is more than 1.5 times the 2021 value. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 1,000 to 1,100, 1,100 to 1,210 and 1,210 to 1,331 are each rises of 10 percent. Statement 2 is correct: 1,331 minus 1,000 is 331, and 331 out of 1,000 is 33.1 percent. Statement 3 is incorrect: 1,331 out of 1,000 is 1.331 times, which is less than 1.5 times.

items.question: Four funds gave returns of 15 percent, 12 percent, 10 percent and 8 percent. A fifth fund gave a return equal to the average of the four. Consider the following statements. (1) The fifth fund's return is 11.25 percent. (2) The funds with 12 percent and 8 percent together exceed the highest return. (3) The fund with 10 percent is exactly halfway between the highest and the lowest returns. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: The average of the four returns is (15 + 12 + 10 + 8)/4 = 11.25%, so the fifth fund returns 11.25%. The 12% and 8% funds together give 20%, which exceeds the highest return of 15%. Halfway between 15% and 8% is 11.5%, not 10%, so the third statement is false. Statements 1 and 2 are correct.

items.question: The economic reforms known as liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation began in 1991. The Securities and Exchange Board of India was given statutory status in 1992. The NITI Aayog was formed in 2015. Consider the following statements. (1) The 1991 reforms came first of the three. (2) The gap between the Securities and Exchange Board of India receiving statutory status and the formation of the NITI Aayog is 23 years. (3) All three happened in the 20th century. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 1991 comes before 1992 and 2015. Statement 2 is correct: 2015 minus 1992 is 23. Statement 3 is incorrect: the NITI Aayog was formed in 2015, which is in the 21st century.

(1) The annual interest on the deposit rises from Rs 28,000 to Rs 30,000. (2) The annual interest rises by Rs 2,000. (3) The new interest is more than the old interest by one-fourteenth of the old interest. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 7 percent of 4 lakh is 28,000 and 7.5 percent of 4 lakh is 30,000. Statement 2 is correct: 30,000 minus 28,000 is 2,000. Statement 3 is correct: 2,000 out of 28,000 is one-fourteenth.

items.question: Share A rises from Rs 100 to Rs 120. Share B rises from Rs 200 to Rs 230. Consider the following statements. (1) Share A rises by 20 percent. (2) Share B rises by 15 percent. (3) Share A rises by more in rupees than share B. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 20 out of 100 is 20 percent. Statement 2 is correct: 30 out of 200 is 15 percent. Statement 3 is incorrect: share A rises by Rs 20 while share B rises by Rs 30, so A rises by less in rupees.

items.question: Per capita income is total national income divided by population. A country's national income is Rs 200 lakh crore and its population is 140 crore. Consider the following statements. (1) Per capita income is about Rs 1,42,857. (2) Per capita income rises if national income rises and population is unchanged. (3) Per capita income is the income of the average person. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: 200 lakh crore divided by 140 crore is about 1,42,857. Statement 2 is correct: dividing a larger income by the same population gives a larger result. Statement 3 is correct: that is what the average means here.

items.question: A firm's exports fell from May, only in shipments to one buyer, while shipments to other buyers were unchanged. Three explanations are offered: a rupee appreciation in April that affected all exporters, a port strike in May that affected all shipments from the port, and the bankruptcy of that one buyer in May. Consider the following statements. (1) The rupee appreciation is ruled out, because it affected all exporters but the fall is only in shipments to one buyer. (2) The port strike is the most likely cause, because the fall began in the same month as the strike. (3) The buyer's bankruptcy is supported as a cause, because the fall matches it in scope and in timing. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
items.explanation: Statement 1 is correct: a change affecting all exporters cannot explain a fall confined to one buyer. Statement 2 is incorrect: the strike affected all shipments from the port, not one buyer only, so the timing coincidence alone does not make it the cause. Statement 3 is correct: the fall is confined to the bankrupt buyer's shipments and began when the buyer went bankrupt.
